newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU shipowners fear shipbuilding subsidy race.
newsitem.headline: EU shipowners fear shipbuilding subsidy race.

text.p: Failure by the United States to ratify an OECD accord to slash shipbuilding support might spark off a race for subsidies which could hit the freight market, a European Union shipowners' body warned on Thursday.
The United States is the only country which has not yet ratified the deal sponsored in 1994 by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development to scrap most state support to shipyards.

"If the U.S. doesn't ratify and there is no new agreement, there is nothing left anymore of the OECD philosophy, then you may indeed end up with a subsidy race," said Alphons Guinier, secretary-general of the European Community Shipowners' Association.

This would be a "disaster for everybody, for shipowners, for shipbuilders," Guinier told Reuters. It could lead to an unhealthy overcapacity on the market for ships which would lead to "a collapse in rates, in charter prices and what have you."
The OECD deal ends direct shipbuilding subsidies except social, and research and development aid. But the prospects for U.S. ratification remain uncertain.
The signatories to the accord, originally due to have come into force in January 1996, are the 15-nation EU, Japan, South Korea, Norway and the United States.
Although the Clinton administration supports the pact, it has been blocked by Congressional attempts to amend it.
Among other things, U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts at the end of the Cold War.

At an OECD meeting on March 12-13, the United States said it would put forward legislation which might lead to ratification and that it would report back on the prospects for this within the next two to three months.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, reacting to U.S. criticism of EU plans to allow $2.1 billion in aid to German, Greek and Spanish shipyards, called on the United States on Wednesday to ratify the OECD deal.
He was responding to a statement by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky expressing "dismay" at the EU proposal to clear the aid.

"Instead of indulging in squabbles over what are non-issues in comparison to the implementation of the OECD agreement, Mr Van Miert calls on the U.S. to fulfil its obligations and ratify the agreement so that it can come into effect as soon as possible," said a statement issued by his office.

Reacting to the Commission's proposal last Wednesday to clear the restructuring aid, Barshefsky said all parties to the OECD deal had clear obligations which they must stick to and that Washington was seeking an explanation from the EU.
"We will be reviewing our course of action in light of their response," she said in a statement last Friday.
But Van Miert said the commitment of the EU to the OECD deal "has materialised in the EU's continuing patience towards the U.S. delay in its international obligations."
He said none of the restructuring cases, originally agreed before the OECD deal was signed, would distort competition.

The EU executive had delayed a decision on the requests by Germany, Spain and Greece to grant the aid, preferring to wait for news of U.S. ratification, but decided to go ahead last Wednesday after the inconclusive OECD meeting in mid-March.

Guinier at the shipowners' association said he had not analysed the cases in detail yet. "But our general view is that one should avoid steps which may possibly further endanger the OECD agreement on shipbuilding," he said.
The EU has extended its rules on aid to the shipbuilding sector until the end of 1997 but has already started thinking about what to do if the OECD deal has not been ratified by then.
